## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- select a Redis structure from an access pattern
- explain expiration, eviction, persistence, and replication as separate concerns
- compare Pub/Sub, Lists, and Streams
- inspect the rental platform's Redis keys and delivery state

## Redis data structures

| Structure | Useful operations | Example use |
|---|---|---|
| String | `GET`, `SET`, `INCR` | Cache entry or counter |
| Hash | Field read and update | Compact object attributes |
| Set | Membership and intersection | Unique tags or eligibility |
| Sorted set | Score range and rank | Time or priority index |
| List | Push, pop, blocking move | Work queue |
| Stream | Append, range, consumer groups | Retained event log |

A Redis key also needs a namespace, ownership rule, lifetime, and size limit.

## Keys and expiration

```text
rental:RENT-42:summary
insurance:RENT-42:offer
auction:events:simple:insurance-service:ready
```

Time-to-live supports expiration. An eviction policy handles memory pressure.
These mechanisms solve different problems: expiration follows application
rules, while eviction protects the Redis instance.

## Atomic operations

Each Redis command executes atomically. Multi-key correctness depends on the
chosen command, transaction, or Lua script and on cluster key placement.

`LMOVE source destination LEFT RIGHT` removes and inserts one element as one
operation. The application still needs a later acknowledgement step after the
business transaction succeeds.

## Persistence and recovery

| Mechanism | Purpose | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| RDB snapshot | Point-in-time dataset | Changes after the snapshot can be lost |
| AOF | Log write operations | More storage and replay work |
| Replication | Maintain copies | Replicas can contain the same logical error |
| Backup | Recover outside the live system | Requires restore testing |

Durability depends on configuration and failure assumptions. Memory speed does
not imply ephemeral-only use, and persistence does not guarantee zero loss.

## Three messaging choices

| Mechanism | Offline consumer | Competing consumers | Replay |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Pub/Sub | No | No queue ownership | No |
| List | Yes while retained | Yes | Manual |
| Stream | Yes while retained | Consumer groups | Range and group position |

The current platform uses Lists. A future module will add Streams in parallel
to compare behavior with the same event contract.

## Redis in the repository

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Publisher[Rental publisher] --> Published[(events:simple:published)]
    Published --> Router[Python event router]
    Router --> RentalQ[(Rental ready list)]
    Router --> InsuranceQ[(Insurance ready list)]
```

PostgreSQL stores durable business state and processed-event identities. Redis
coordinates delivery.

## Operational questions

- Which keys can grow without a bound?
- Which data can expire safely?
- What happens after Redis restarts?
- Which commands reveal queue depth and stuck processing?
- Which business records allow reconciliation after message loss?

Answers belong in runbooks and monitoring, not only in application code.
